consumer_seed: The Ofcom business-contracts page was published on 21 September 2015.
The Ofcom business-contracts page was last updated on 26 June 2026.
Ofcom advises businesses to check whether the monthly amount stays the same over the contract.
Ofcom advises checking the offered minimum contract period and the notice period required by the provider.
Ofcom advises checking rights if agreed terms change or prices rise unexpectedly.
A contract may use a single fixed monthly price for its full term.
A contract may start at one monthly price and increase on a specified date.
The monthly amount payable during the contract should be provided clearly before sign-up.
If a provider raises prices beyond what was agreed, it must give at least one month's notice.
If a provider raises prices beyond what was agreed, the customer should have a right to exit without penalty.
Planned in-contract price rises should be made clear at the point of sale.
Providers must clearly state the post-rise price in pounds and pence.
Providers must clearly state when a planned price rise will occur.
A clearly disclosed agreed price rise does not create a penalty-free exit right when it occurs.
Businesses can ask for specified contract information in a clear, comprehensible and easily accessible form.
Requested contract information can include whether services may be limited or restricted.
Requested contract information can include minimum service quality and initial connection time.
Requested contract information can include customer-service and maintenance arrangements.
Requested contract information can include contract length and renewal conditions.
Requested contract information can include termination charges, including early termination charges.
A provider must give a small business with ten employees or fewer key contract information before sign-up.
The pre-contract summary is one page, or three pages for bundled services.
The contract summary includes charges, contract length and the cancellation process.
Before the customer is bound, the provider must supply more detailed contract information in writing.
Disabled customers can request contract information in a reasonably acceptable format such as large print or Braille.
Businesses should consider extra charges such as paper billing, roaming, early exit and insufficient cancellation notice.
An automatically renewable contract rolls into a new minimum period unless the customer opts out.
For small-business landline or broadband services, the provider must obtain consent for each new minimum contract period.
A small-business contract with ten employees or fewer should not exceed 24 months.
A small-business contract should not be extended when additional services are bought unless the customer consents.
Provider termination procedures should not make changing provider more difficult.
A service level agreement defines service terms and support or problem-resolution arrangements.
An SLA may cover repair times, complaint response, coverage, connection speed and maximum days without service.
Service level guarantees commonly include compensation arrangements when the SLA is not met.
The Ofcom new-contract checklist was published on 22 January 2014.
The Ofcom new-contract checklist was last updated on 26 June 2026.
The checklist is aimed at residential and small-business customers with ten employees or fewer.
Some contracts are rolling and can be cancelled month to month.
Other contracts commonly tie customers in for 12, 18 or 24 months.
Providers must offer a contract option no longer than 12 months for each service they provide.
A residential or small-business service contract should be no longer than 24 months.
A longer mobile-handset contract must be separate from the airtime contract.
The mobile airtime contract cannot be longer than 24 months.
Leaving a 12-, 18- or 24-month contract early will usually involve a charge.
Early termination charges should not exceed the payments remaining on the contract.
A contract may use a fixed monthly price for the full term.
A contract may state a starting price and a higher price from a specified date.
The monthly amount payable should be stated clearly before sign-up.
A price rise beyond the agreed terms requires at least one month's notice.
A price rise beyond the agreed terms requires a penalty-free exit right.
A planned rise must be clearly disclosed at the point of sale in pounds and pence with its timing.
A rise disclosed at sign-up does not create a penalty-free exit right when applied.
Customers should check usage allowances and charges for exceeding them.
Customers should check extra costs such as paper bills, caller ID, voicemail and non-direct-debit payment.
Customers should check fault-repair timescales, compensation, redress and engineer-visit charges.
Ofcom recommends its accredited price-comparison sites when checking available deals.
Ofcom's provider-choice information includes complaints and overall satisfaction rates.
A provider must give key contract information before the customer signs up.
Before consent, the customer should receive a written one-page summary or three pages for a bundle.
The summary includes charges, contract length and the cancellation process.
The provider must also give detailed written contract information before the customer is bound.
A broadband buyer should receive accurate information about expected broadband speed.
For fixed broadband, providers should explain minimum, normally available, maximum and advertised download and upload speeds.
For mobile broadband, providers should explain estimated maximum and advertised download and upload speeds.
A customer who believes a contract change was not properly notified or was mis-sold should make a formal complaint.
Ofcom advises asking for a reference number when making a complaint.
An unresolved complaint may be eligible for ADR after six weeks or earlier at deadlock.
The provider must identify its ADR scheme, and Ofcom also provides an ADR checker.
expansion_rule: Join Wave151 December values to Wave155 January values by normalized contract name. For each of 37 contracts emit sixteen records: contracted delta, built delta or missing guard, built percentage change or missing/zero-base guard, December built ratio, January built ratio or missing guard, ratio-point change or missing guard, December and January shares of displayed contracted totals, December and January shares of displayed built totals or missing guard, December and January contracted ranks, December and January built ranks or missing guard, change in unbuilt gap, and a combined continuity classification. Append 68 Ofcom contract and checklist records. Equal numeric values share competition rank. Every fifth expanded record is REVALIDATION; all others are UPGRADE.
